title: Hank's Contract

jokes.text: The worst thing you can do is box a left-hander. They're put on backwards as it is.
jokes.setup: Larry and George Foreman are discussing boxing strategy on-air
jokes.punchline: George delivers the absurd folk-wisdom that left-handers are 'put on backwards as it is' — as if it's obvious common sense
jokes.explanation: George Foreman's delivery of pseudo-scientific boxing logic as plain fact is funny because of its confident absurdity. 'Put on backwards' is a vivid, odd phrase. Works as character comedy from a real celebrity playing himself.

dialogue.speaker: George
dialogue.line: The worst thing you can do is box a left-hander. Why? They're put on backwards as it is.

jokes.text: Hank is getting ready to drop his contract, so I might as well get him.
jokes.setup: Larry has been insisting all week that Hank is not leaving; George casually treats Hank like a future boxing opponent
jokes.punchline: George pivots from boxing talk to offer to literally fight Hank as though it's a natural segue
jokes.explanation: The joke works because George is treating Hank's contract dispute as if it's a boxing opportunity — absurd celebrity-logic that plays well with Foreman's folksy persona. The casual pivot is economical and slightly subversive.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Wouldn't that prepare you properly? That's a great idea.

dialogue.speaker: George
dialogue.line: I wasn't born yesterday. I never thought about that.

jokes.text: That Hank is not leaving the network. He is in contract negotiations. He is not leaving the show. He's in contract negotiations.
jokes.setup: Larry insists he is calm about the negotiations
jokes.punchline: His over-insistence and repetition reveal the exact anxiety he's denying — classic Larry Sanders self-undermining
jokes.explanation: Larry's verbal spiraling is pure character comedy. The humor is in the gap between his claimed composure and his compulsive repetition. Very Larry Sanders — the self-deception is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: you'll agree with me... I don't think I should cave in, right?

dialogue.speaker: George
dialogue.line: No, not at all. Belly-bump or do something.

jokes.text: Boy, oh, boy, Chef Paul's gumbo was incredibly strong. Steam coming out of my ass, Arty.
jokes.setup: The post-show debrief begins as a normal conversation about the show
jokes.punchline: Shel barges in complaining about explosive digestive distress from the gumbo — total non-sequitur delivered with executive authority
jokes.explanation: 'Steam coming out of my ass, Arty' is blunt, vivid, and delivered without apology or embarrassment — which is exactly what makes it funny. The contrast between Shel's institutional authority and this overshare is sharp. Quotable line.

dialogue.line: Steam coming out of my ass, Arty.

jokes.text: You could sit and talk to them. You think that'd be less painful?
jokes.setup: Larry complains about having to cook something every time a chef is on the show
jokes.punchline: Artie's comeback implies that merely talking to the chef guest would itself be painful — a dry put-down of both the show's format and celebrity guests in general
jokes.explanation: Artie's line is sharp and economical. It's meta-commentary on the tedium of celebrity interviews disguised as a simple retort. The implication that cooking is better than talking is a darkly funny inversion of TV hospitality. Very Artie.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: At the moment, the latest demand is a golf cart to drive around the studio. Poor deluded bastard.

jokes.text: The latest demand is a golf cart to drive around the studio. Poor deluded bastard.
jokes.setup: Shel is cataloguing Hank's contract demands
jokes.punchline: The golf cart demand is already absurdly humble, and 'poor deluded bastard' adds condescending pity — Hank is being pathetic without even knowing it
jokes.explanation: This joke works on multiple levels: the bathos of Hank's most audacious demand being a golf cart, Shel's total lack of self-awareness about his own cruelty, and the word 'deluded' adding a psychiatric dimension. 'Poor deluded bastard' is quotable and perfectly captures the show's tone — industry power figures casually grinding down the less powerful.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: My dog wouldn't eat that shit.

jokes.text: Of course, basically, that's exactly what you two do when you're renegotiating your contract.
jokes.setup: Shel is criticizing Hank for claiming to have other offers during negotiations
jokes.punchline: Shel turns it around and points out Larry and Artie do the exact same thing — neutralizing Larry's moral high ground
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant — Shel pulls the rug on Larry's self-righteousness, which is a recurring pleasure of the series. The hypocrisy reveal is gentle but lands because it immediately triggers Larry's defensive spiral.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Do you think that stain on his pants is from the gumbo? I don't think so.

jokes.text: Now, wait a minute. I had an offer last year... I could have gone on after Nightline.
jokes.setup: Shel implies Larry bluffs during negotiations just like Hank
jokes.punchline: Larry's instant, over-insistent defensiveness about the Nightline offer (which we later learn was a bluff) is perfectly timed — the audience may already suspect the lie
jokes.explanation: This moment gains enormous rewatch value because it's the first plant of the Nightline bluff that pays off at the end. In the moment it's a solid character beat; in retrospect it's beautifully constructed dramatic irony. Larry's insistence is pure character.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Kenny Stabler? He played football. Basketball. I didn't have any spare footballs around when he was on the show... so it's the closest kind of ball I could find.

jokes.text: It's not you, Shel. It's that gumbo. My dog wouldn't eat that shit.
jokes.setup: Larry apologizes to Shel for his irritability about the contract talk
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots to blaming the gumbo, with the dog comparison adding escalating contempt
jokes.explanation: A mild callback to Shel's gumbo line that continues the running complaint. The dog comparison is a nice escalation of contempt, but it's not a particularly inventive joke — more of a connective tissue gag keeping the gumbo thread alive.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: How do you place a value on a man who introduces Wynnona Judd as 'TheJudd'?

jokes.text: Do you think that stain on his pants is from the gumbo? I don't think so.
jokes.setup: Hank and Shel are walking away in the hallway, in the middle of a serious business conversation
jokes.punchline: Larry (or Artie) spots an unidentified stain on Hank's pants and speculates it isn't from food — darkly implying something more embarrassing
jokes.explanation: The visual gag is inferred — we see Hank walking away and the observers notice the stain. The 'I don't think so' is doing all the work as a deadpan insinuation. Punches down at Hank but not cruelly enough to feel mean-spirited.

dialogue.line: She was... Jane Russell?

jokes.text: Don't I have enough pressure on me with everything without worrying about what you were like when you were 30 and who you dated?
jokes.setup: Artie apparently starts telling a story about when he was 30 and a woman he knew
jokes.punchline: Larry's preemptive shut-down reveals his self-absorption — he can't even hear Artie's tangent without making it about his own stress
jokes.explanation: Pure Larry Sanders character comedy — his narcissism expressed as exhaustion at having to process other people's reminiscences. The specificity of the complaint ('what you were like when you were 30 and who you dated') makes it funnier than a generic dismissal.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Fuck it, it's free cake. We can't miss this.

jokes.text: Does the name Kim Novak mean anything? Get outta here.
jokes.setup: Larry has just told Artie not to talk about who he dated at 30
jokes.punchline: Artie drops 'Kim Novak' as if it's a mic-drop — the name alone is the joke, implying a spectacular story Larry now has to live without knowing
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's first genuinely excellent joke. Artie's economy is perfect: two words do all the work. 'Kim Novak' is precisely the right vintage-Hollywood name to make the story instantly legendary, and Larry's 'Get outta here' is the perfect straight-man reaction. The joke is entirely about what we don't hear. Artie as a man of mystery who has lived an extraordinary life is crucial character integration — only Artie could deliver this. Could only work with this specific character on this specific show.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: If someone invented a camera that could take, you know, snapshots of our feelings... I would take a picture of this moment and keep it in the wallet of my heart forever.

jokes.text: Yeah, but Kenny Stabler? He played football... Basketball... I know.
jokes.setup: Artie presents Hank with an autographed Kenny Stabler basketball — he couldn't find a football when the player was on the show
jokes.punchline: Larry corrects 'football' to 'basketball' — he doesn't even know what sport Kenny Stabler played — before Artie confirms both of them are wrong (Stabler played football, not basketball)
jokes.explanation: The confusion about sports is a gentle comedy of competence — nobody on a talk show actually knows or cares about sports specifics. The three-beat structure (football / basketball correction / 'I know') is cleanly executed. More industry-insider humor about the hollowness of the celebrity memorabilia exchange.

dialogue.line: I say he goes right into the cruise director story.
Bet you a hundred bucks it's the telephone story.

jokes.text: You should thank Arty anyway. He's the one who wrote it. He put it on the cards for me. I just read it off the cards. Where it would have stayed had you not read it.
jokes.setup: Hank thanks Larry for the heartfelt tribute Larry gave him on-air
jokes.punchline: Larry deflects to Artie; Artie deflects back with a passive-aggressive couplet — 'where it would have stayed had you not read it' — which is simultaneously a compliment and an insult to Larry
jokes.explanation: Artie's comeback is beautifully structured — it starts as a compliment to Hank and pivots to a dig at Larry's autopilot delivery, all without raising his voice. 'Where it would have stayed' is the kind of line veteran TV comedy writers get right. It also reveals the mechanical nature of 'sincere' on-air moments, which is the show's central thesis.

dialogue.line: Every time we have a going-away party for you, it's just too much of a downer.

jokes.text: How do you place a value on a man who introduces Wynonna Judd as 'The Judd'?
jokes.setup: Artie and Larry are mocking Hank's perceived value to the show
jokes.punchline: Larry's specific example of Hank's incompetence — introducing Wynonna as 'The Judd' — is both a real insult and accidental poetry
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The specificity of 'The Judd' is perfect — it captures Hank's haplessness (forgetting the name, defaulting to the article), the absurdity of the music industry's branding, and Larry's exasperated affection all at once. Only Larry Sanders would frame this as a philosophical question about human value. Highly quotable, character-specific, economical. Close to an 8 anchor-quality line.

dialogue.speaker: Barbara
dialogue.line: That number you gave me was to some dry cleaner's in Torrance.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Yeah, the area code got changed.

dialogue.speaker: Barbara
dialogue.line: Bullshit. I am not your whore.

jokes.text: That was a low point, even for him, wasn't it? I'm surprised she came out. She was... Jane Russell?
jokes.setup: They're discussing the 'The Judd' incident
jokes.punchline: Artie trails off and confuses Wynonna Judd with Jane Russell — a Hollywood actress from the 1950s — showing he's equally out of touch but in a different generation
jokes.explanation: Artie confusing Wynonna Judd with Jane Russell is a character-specific joke: he's from a different era and gets celebrities wrong in an older-Hollywood way. It's a self-undermining follow-up to his mockery of Hank, suggesting they're all equally incompetent, just differently.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: People see you in enough of those lawn furniture spots... they tend to fantasize about you.

jokes.text: Isn't he taking this a little seriously this time? Fuck it, it's free cake. We can't miss this.
jokes.setup: A staff member invites Larry and Artie to Hank's going-away cake; Larry wonders if it's real
jokes.punchline: Artie cuts through Larry's sentimentality with pure pragmatism — free cake overrides all ethical considerations
jokes.explanation: 'Fuck it, it's free cake. We can't miss this.' is a beautifully Artie line — all the philosophical ambiguity of the situation resolved by the economics of complimentary baked goods. Economy score is nearly perfect; every word is load-bearing. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Why do I need this car anyway? I already have a car.

dialogue.speaker: Car salesman
dialogue.line: 'Cause you deserve it. It's safer, and it's classier.

jokes.text: White cake with coconut sprinkles?
jokes.setup: Hank is being secretly coordinated with over the phone for his own surprise party
jokes.punchline: Hank asks about the specific cake flavor — he's being lured to his own surprise party and is entirely focused on the dessert details
jokes.explanation: Hank's vanity and self-focus means he's primarily concerned about the quality of his own going-away cake. It's a small but perfectly calibrated character moment — Hank is being played but is also playing himself.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: let Arty and I take care of the strippers... because we can probably find one that doesn't know you.

jokes.text: If someone invented a camera that could take snapshots of our feelings, I would take a picture of this moment and keep it in the wallet of my heart forever.
jokes.setup: Hank has been surprised by his going-away party and begins an emotional speech
jokes.punchline: The 'wallet of my heart' metaphor is so overwrought and mixed that it becomes inadvertent self-parody — Hank is completely sincere, which makes it more painful
jokes.explanation: The 'wallet of my heart' is a peak Hank Kingsley moment — grandiose, incoherent, utterly sincere. Jeffrey Tambor playing this completely straight is what makes it devastating rather than merely silly. The metaphor itself ('a camera... for feelings') starts badly and the 'wallet of my heart' finish is a spectacular collapse. Only Hank would say this. One of the episode's most quotable and characterful lines.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: She was half theJudds. Now there's just one of them, so she's a... she is a Judd. She is a singleJudd!

jokes.text: Knowing most of you... most of you... has been a great pleasure.
jokes.setup: Hank is continuing his going-away speech with sentiment
jokes.punchline: The self-correction — 'most of you... MOST of you' — reveals there are people in the room he doesn't like, mid-compliment, and he won't pretend otherwise
jokes.explanation: The repetition of 'most of you' with a meaningful pause between them is a perfect cringe comedy beat. Hank is trying to be gracious but his pettiness leaks through. The joke is in the rhythm — the first 'most of you' sounds like it's building to something warm; the second 'most of you' confirms he's hedging. The audience/staff is presumably visible squirming. Superb economy: the whole joke is in a single three-word repetition.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: What about the time I chipped my tooth on the bathroom urinal? What the fuck is so comical about that?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: It was a back tooth, Hank. I don't know how you did it.

jokes.text: The powers that be want to put a price on what we have here, and I'm afraid that price is just too low.
jokes.setup: Hank's going-away speech continues with sincere grievance
jokes.punchline: The accidental self-awareness of 'the price is too low' — Hank is inadvertently admitting he's a commodity being undervalued, which is literally true but not what he means to be saying
jokes.explanation: Hank's rhetoric accidentally cuts to the industry truth he's trying to obscure — he IS just being priced. The gap between his intended eloquence and what he's actually saying is the joke. Pure Larry Sanders show-business pathos.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: That was the speaker phone. Nice try.

jokes.text: I say he goes right into the cruise director story. Bet you a hundred bucks it's the telephone story. You're on.
jokes.setup: Hank is winding up into a long personal anecdote during his speech
jokes.punchline: Larry and Artie immediately start side-betting on which of Hank's repetitive stock stories he'll tell — implying they've heard them all many times and track them like weather patterns
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best structural jokes. The bet establishes that Hank has a finite repertoire of sad anecdotes that everyone around him has memorized. The fact that Larry and Artie immediately gamble on which story is coming is both a devastating commentary on Hank's self-absorption and a genuinely funny character bit for Larry and Artie's relationship. 'You're on' is perfectly timed. The payoff when Hank starts the cruise director story and Artie loses is excellent scene construction.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: When you let one go, boy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hello. That was the speaker phone.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Nice try.

jokes.text: On the Andropolis. The Andropolis, let me fill you in, was a Greek liner. It was a luxury...
jokes.setup: Hank has started the cruise director story as Larry predicted
jokes.punchline: Hank begins elaborately setting up the backstory with 'let me fill you in' — as if anyone asked — showing he's completely unaware that his audience has heard this before
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the cruise director bet. 'Let me fill you in' is perfect oblivious Hank — presenting well-worn material as exclusive insider knowledge. The joke's strength depends on the setup at 07:51.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I was eating a sandwich in my office when suddenly I heard you guys.

jokes.text: Hank's speech is interrupted and a stripper pops out of a large cake — going-away party revealed as a surprise sex party
jokes.setup: Hank's going-away speech has been building; the party seemed to be a genuine emotional farewell
jokes.punchline: The going-away party is actually a surprise stripper-cake party, cutting off Hank's cruise director story mid-sentence
jokes.explanation: The structural payoff is that the stripper cuts off Hank's story — the exact moment everyone was dreading. The transition from earnest pathos to stripper entertainment is a tonal whiplash that works. Also confirms the staff's casual cruelty toward Hank.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I'm tired of being your personal village idiot.

jokes.text: Thank you. I had no idea that you and Paul could... Phil. Could be so, you know, openly expressive about your affection.
jokes.setup: Hank responds to the stripper reveal by trying to be gracious
jokes.punchline: Hank gets the organizer's name wrong (Paul/Phil) and then wraps the whole thing in a bizarre euphemism — 'openly expressive about your affection' — for hiring a stripper
jokes.explanation: Hank getting the name wrong while delivering his emotional thank-you speech is a well-timed puncture. 'Openly expressive about your affection' is a great Hank-ism — his pompous register applied to a stripper situation. Character-specific and earned.

dialogue.speaker: Robin Williams
dialogue.line: If men carried the baby, wouldn't it? He'd be like, 'I got things to do. Get it out! Yeah, right, okay. Yeah, okay, I see it. Come on.'

jokes.text: Well... it's very nice to meet you. Meet me? You've done a hell of a lot more than meet me.
jokes.setup: Hank says 'it's very nice to meet you' to the stripper as she emerges from the cake
jokes.punchline: The stripper reveals she and Hank have a history — he's pretending not to know her in front of everyone
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured misdirection — Hank's polite 'nice to meet you' is revealed as a desperate cover-up. 'You've done a hell of a lot more than meet me' is the perfect comeback: explicit, economical, and damning. The escalation into full public humiliation makes this one of the episode's best moments. Very high craft — the setup and subversion are both excellent, and the character specificity is perfect for Hank.

dialogue.speaker: Robin Williams
dialogue.line: It's just too damn easy. He looks like a before from Hair Club.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I can't go with you on that. I cannot.

jokes.text: You asshole. That number you gave me was to some dry cleaner's in Torrance. Yeah, the area code got changed. I don't know how come. Bullshit. I am not your whore.
jokes.setup: The stripper has already revealed she knows Hank; now she confronts him publicly
jokes.punchline: The confrontation escalates through Hank's weak excuse (area code got changed) to her declaration 'I am not your whore' — a nuclear public humiliation
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'nice to meet you' pretense to 'I am not your whore' screamed at a work party is a masterclass in cringe comedy. Hank's excuse — 'the area code got changed' — is so transparently weak it's almost sympathetic. The line 'I am not your whore' in the middle of a professional going-away party is devastating. High impact, high craft. One of the episode's top moments.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: my head reminded you of your penis after a cold swim... I was honored.

jokes.text: People see you in enough of those lawn furniture spots, they tend to fantasize about you.
jokes.setup: After the stripper confrontation, Hank is humiliated and Larry tries to explain/deflect
jokes.punchline: Larry's explanation — that Hank's lawn furniture commercials have made him a sex symbol — is both an insult disguised as a compliment and absurdist commentary on celebrity
jokes.explanation: This line is exceptional. 'Lawn furniture spots' is the specific, deflating detail that makes it — not just commercials, not even furniture commercials, but *lawn furniture* commercials. The implication that this is Hank's entire cultural footprint as a sex symbol is both cruel and precise. Larry's delivery of it as sincere consolation makes it even better. One of the episode's most quotable lines and finest examples of the show's industry-insider cruelty.

dialogue.speaker: Robin Williams
dialogue.line: He's hung like a field mouse. It's like a little sundial. Honey, what time is it? Get the baby. It's 3:00. Oh, 2:30 now. It's real cold.

jokes.text: Does the LXE have a limited slip differential? ...What is the limited slip differential? ...Why do I need this car anyway? I already have a car.
jokes.setup: Hank is on the phone negotiating a car purchase, a symbol of his new contract demands
jokes.punchline: Hank negotiates with increasing confusion until he admits he doesn't know what he's asking for and questions the premise entirely
jokes.explanation: Hank's car phone negotiation is a great character sequence — he's bluffing about knowing automotive terminology just as he's bluffing about his value to the network. The progression from confident to confused to 'why do I need this anyway' mirrors his larger situation perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Don't you know? No, my TV stops at channel 13... the way it's supposed to.

jokes.text: Maury Povich, yeah. Thank you.
jokes.setup: Hank hangs up his car phone call
jokes.punchline: He addresses the salesperson as 'Maury Povich' — seemingly either he got a different call, or he's so distracted he's confused the car dealer with the TV host
jokes.explanation: The Maury Povich non-sequitur is a perfectly placed absurdist button. The audience has no idea why he said it, which is exactly right — it's Hank's world of TV celebrity bleeding into everything. Economy is near-perfect: the name alone lands the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hey, you untalented, overpriced sidekick... you're just another piece of meat to us... so why don't you take what we gave you last year and be happy with that... you worthless piece of shit?

jokes.text: Don't leave me alone with Hank. I'll be listening on the speaker phone. I'll be with you spiritually.
jokes.setup: Larry panics about having to meet alone with Hank to discuss negotiations
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'I'll be with you spiritually' is both a genuine deadpan and a plant for the speakerphone reveal — though framed as a joke, it's literally what he does
jokes.explanation: This is structurally the best joke in the episode. 'I'll be with you spiritually' functions perfectly as a dry comic deflection and as a literal foreshadowing of what Artie actually does. On rewatch, it's extraordinary — the joke and the plot are the same line. Pure Artie character: warm paternal irony that turns out to be literal. Economy and structure are both excellent. Among the episode's finest moments.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: There's no Cavett. You hear me? Zip on Cavett. I'm bluffing.

jokes.text: Talk to Shel recently? About anything in particular? No, about my hair weave. About my leaving.
jokes.setup: Larry asks Hank if he's talked to Shel, hoping to ease into the conversation
jokes.punchline: Hank's sarcastic 'No, about my hair weave' — first offering the most absurd possible subject before landing on the real one — is a great character line that also confirms Hank is aware of/sensitive about his hair
jokes.explanation: Hank's hair weave is a recurring character vulnerability, so 'about my hair weave' as a sarcastic deflection is deeply character-specific. The beat structure (absurd option / real option) is clean. Hank is sharp when cornered — this is the more intelligent Hank that makes him sympathetic as well as comic.

dialogue.speaker: Shel
dialogue.line: It's that golf cart I told you about last week.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I smell urine here.

jokes.text: Next year, when we have the going-away party, let Arty and I take care of the strippers, because we can probably find one that doesn't know you.
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to smooth things over with Hank after the stripper disaster
jokes.punchline: His 'apology' is to offer to find a stripper Hank hasn't already slept with — which presupposes Hank has a deep bench of sex worker acquaintances
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's single funniest line. The callback to the stripper incident is perfectly constructed: Larry's 'solution' is to vet future strippers against Hank's existing rolodex of sex workers. The implication is both devastating and affectionate — Larry is essentially saying 'we know exactly who you are, Hank.' 'Doesn't know you' is brilliant economy. The joke lands on multiple levels simultaneously and would get a big laugh from any comedy-savvy room.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I don't mean on these stairs. I mean, you know, the network.

jokes.text: A woman I happen to have met pops out of a very large present.
jokes.setup: Hank is still trying to claim he merely 'met' the stripper after being publicly exposed
jokes.punchline: His euphemistic formulation — 'a woman I happen to have met' — is desperately thin given what just occurred; 'pops out of a very large present' is the most clinical possible description of a stripper emerging from a cake
jokes.explanation: Hank maintaining his cover story with the flimsiest possible language is perfectly in character. 'A woman I happen to have met' is a beautiful euphemism that fools no one. His maintaining the thin pretense while everyone is in on the joke is the essence of Hank comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I had to pay for it myself, so don't tell anybody, okay?

jokes.text: She was half the Judds. Now there's just one of them, so she is a Judd. She is a single Judd!
jokes.setup: Hank objects to Larry and Artie laughing about the 'The Judd' incident
jokes.punchline: Larry clarifies the math: after Naomi left due to illness, Wynonna became the entirety of a formerly two-person brand, which creates the inadvertently logical 'single Judd' formulation
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'The Judd' pays off brilliantly here. 'She is a single Judd!' delivered with Larry's triumphant logic is one of the episode's best lines. It's a factual observation presented as a joke — the humor comes from the ruthless grammatical reasoning applied to a real person's family tragedy. Highly quotable, character-specific, and builds on the earlier joke to new heights.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You got a very different way of showing your love, don't you?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I've seen men be burned in dark interiors.

jokes.text: What about the time I chipped my tooth on the bathroom urinal? What the fuck is so comical about that?
jokes.setup: Hank is cataloguing ways Larry and Artie have laughed at him
jokes.punchline: The bathroom urinal tooth incident is such a specific, baffling, embarrassing injury that the mere revelation stops the scene — we don't know how it happened and that's the point
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's most purely funny moment. 'What about the time I chipped my tooth on the bathroom urinal? What the fuck is so comical about that?' is brilliant on every level. The incident itself is absurdly specific and horrible — a back-tooth injury on a urinal implies a very particular kind of embarrassing accident that is never explained. The defensive follow-up ('what the fuck is so comical') only makes it funnier because the answer is obviously 'everything.' Only Hank would have this injury AND lead with it as a grievance AND be bewildered by the reaction. Approaches anchor quality — vivid, quotable, character-specific, earned. The pause before Artie's response is the cherry on top.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You did have that offer to go on after Nightline, didn't you?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Fuck no.

jokes.text: It was a back tooth, Hank. [beat] I don't know how you did it.
jokes.setup: Hank has just mentioned chipping his tooth on a bathroom urinal
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'It was a back tooth, Hank' — delivered as if this changes anything — followed by the genuine bewilderment of 'I don't know how you did it' is the perfect reaction beat
jokes.explanation: This reaction beat is near-perfect comedy writing. 'It was a back tooth, Hank' implies Larry has been worrying about the mechanics of this incident for years. The specificity of the back-tooth correction — as if this detail redeems or explains anything — is absurd and wonderful. The follow-up 'I don't know how you did it' is Larry breaking from deflection into genuine curiosity, and the pause before it is where the laugh lives. This two-line sequence earns its high score: maximum economy, perfect structure, and could ONLY be Larry Sanders responding to ONLY Hank. Comparable to the best anchor examples.

jokes.text: You cut one? What the hell was that? [beat] That was the speaker phone.
jokes.setup: Hank and Larry are having a tense emotional conversation about respect and feeling used
jokes.punchline: A noise interrupts the scene; Larry initially thinks Hank passed gas; Hank corrects him with the speakerphone explanation — which only partially resolves the confusion
jokes.explanation: The tonal whiplash from emotional confrontation to 'you cut one?' is perfectly timed. The setup for the Artie speakerphone reveal is handled well — the 'fart' misdirection is a classic sitcom move, but the show subverts it immediately. The rewatch value is in knowing Artie is on the phone and that he definitely didn't fart.

jokes.text: Nice try. No, someone's listening to our conversation on the speaker phone.
jokes.setup: Larry suggests it was the speaker phone, not Hank passing gas
jokes.punchline: Hank's 'Nice try' — he thinks Larry is covering for a fart with the speakerphone excuse — and then he actually becomes paranoid about surveillance
jokes.explanation: Hank's 'Nice try' is a great beat — he's convinced Larry is covering up a fart while simultaneously being right about the speakerphone for different reasons. The paranoia then becomes real, which is the joke's payoff.

jokes.text: It's me, Larry, Arthur. [long pause]
jokes.setup: Hank has confronted the speaker phone, demanding to know who's listening
jokes.punchline: Artie's matter-of-fact 'It's me, Larry, Arthur' — using his formal name, completely unashamed — followed by the weight of the silence as everyone processes this
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the speakerphone setup is executed perfectly. 'It's me, Larry, Arthur' — identifying himself by first and last name to his closest colleague, with utter calm — is a masterpiece of deadpan. Artie is never embarrassed, never defensive; his complete self-possession in an absurd situation is both funny and definitive of his character. The pause after is where the comedy lives. Only Rip Torn's Artie could deliver this line this way. Very high craft.

jokes.text: I don't know. I have no idea how I got on the phone. I was eating a sandwich in my office when suddenly I heard you guys.
jokes.setup: Larry asks how Artie got on the speaker phone
jokes.punchline: Artie's completely implausible excuse — he was eating a sandwich and accidentally hit a button and happened to be listening to their private conversation — delivered with total earnestness
jokes.explanation: Artie's excuse is funny because it's technically just plausible enough while being obviously false, and he delivers it with complete conviction. 'I was eating a sandwich' as the alibi is wonderfully mundane. The show never confirms whether Artie intended to listen — the ambiguity is the joke. Artie's relationship with truth is one of the show's recurring pleasures.

jokes.text: How's my old buddy, Hank? [offered while clearly listening in]
jokes.setup: Artie has been caught eavesdropping on the private conversation
jokes.punchline: Having been exposed, Artie pivots immediately to warm social pleasantries — 'How's my old buddy, Hank?' — as if the surveillance is now the basis for a catch-up chat
jokes.explanation: Artie pivoting from caught-eavesdropper to warm collegial check-in is perfectly in character. The audacity of 'How's my old buddy, Hank?' after being caught is Artie at his most shameless and brilliant. The show's best character comedy comes from Artie's unflappable confidence in any situation.

jokes.text: I'm tired of being your personal village idiot.
jokes.setup: Hank delivers his ultimatum about leaving the show after feeling disrespected
jokes.punchline: 'Village idiot' is the exact right register — it's both a self-aware and a self-pitying complaint, and the word 'personal' makes it somehow more specific and more devastating
jokes.explanation: One of Hank's finest lines in the episode. 'Personal village idiot' is an unusually precise and self-aware formulation — it admits his function while protesting it, and the 'personal' modifier suggests that Larry has a monopoly on his humiliation. It's funny because it's accurate and because Hank, in his anger, has articulated exactly what he is. Highly quotable, character-specific, economical.

jokes.text: I didn't actually have the baby, but my wife did. It'd be different if men carried the baby, wouldn't it? He'd be like, 'I got things to do. Get it out! Yeah, right, okay.'
jokes.setup: Guest Robin Williams is discussing his new baby on the talk show
jokes.punchline: Williams riffs on men being impatient if they had to carry babies — doing a quick character voice of a man rushing through pregnancy
jokes.explanation: Generic late-night improv riff — the 'men would be impatient if pregnant' premise is well-worn. Williams' energy elevates it but the writing itself is functional rather than distinctive. This is below the episode average in craft because it's generic talk-show material rather than the show's signature dry industry comedy.

jokes.text: It'd be different if men carried the baby, wouldn't it? He'd be like, 'I got things to do. Get it out! Yeah, right, okay. Yeah, okay, I see it. Come on.'
jokes.setup: Robin muses about what it would be like if men carried babies
jokes.punchline: The voice and impatience of a man demanding his own birth be sped up
jokes.explanation: Standard Williams improv riff — competent physical/voice comedy but the concept isn't particularly fresh. The 'men pregnancy' observation was already well-worn by 1992. Functional filler.

jokes.text: We'll be right back. You come back, or you're dead.
jokes.setup: Larry says 'We'll be right back' to end the segment
jokes.punchline: Williams throws in a gleefully menacing 'you come back or you're dead' to the camera — breaking the polite TV formality with violent threat
jokes.explanation: Robin Williams playing himself as manic talk show guest who escalates 'come back after the break' into a death threat is solid. The economy is excellent — five words subvert the entire TV commercial break convention. Williams playing himself is always interesting in this context.

jokes.text: Delightful, Robin, delightful. Sir, your mind is a national treasure.
jokes.setup: Robin has just done a short, fairly modest riff about babies
jokes.punchline: Larry's over-the-top backstage validation — 'your mind is a national treasure' — for what was a mild bit, revealing Larry's compulsive sycophancy with big guests
jokes.explanation: A sharp industry-insider joke. 'Your mind is a national treasure' is disproportionate to what Robin just did, which reveals Larry's professional people-pleasing. The contrast between his treatment of Hank (contempt) and Williams (reverence) is the satirical engine of the show firing perfectly.

jokes.text: Enough of the bullshit. How am I really doing? ...You're Robin Williams. You aren't aware of that? If I was you, I'd never ask how I was doing.
jokes.setup: After the on-air segment, Williams asks Larry how he really did
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'You're Robin Williams. You aren't aware of that?' is a gently baffled response to celebrity insecurity — the absurdity of Robin Williams needing reassurance
jokes.explanation: The backstage celebrity insecurity is perfectly captured here. Larry's incredulous 'You're Robin Williams. You aren't aware of that?' is both funny and touching — it's the show's thesis about celebrity neurosis stated directly. The meta quality of real Robin Williams asking if he did well is part of the joke.

jokes.text: How am I really doing? / You're Robin Williams. You aren't aware of that? If I was you, I'd never ask how I was doing.
jokes.setup: Robin asks for honest feedback about his performance
jokes.punchline: Larry's response is that asking for feedback when you're Robin Williams is absurd — the insecurity reads as false modesty from someone at that level
jokes.explanation: A good meta-showbiz moment. The comedy is in the extreme confidence-gap: Larry is one of the most insecure characters on television telling Robin Williams not to be insecure. The irony of who is offering this advice is implicit but rich.

jokes.text: Oh, man. If you were me, you wouldn't be wearing this suit, I guess. I don't look like an Irish pimp?
jokes.setup: Larry tells Williams he'd never ask how he did if he were him
jokes.punchline: Williams' self-deprecating riff about his suit — 'I don't look like an Irish pimp?' — is the kind of quick-turn absurdist image Williams deploys naturally
jokes.explanation: 'Irish pimp' is a good Williams image — specific enough to be funny — but it's fairly standard Williams improv energy. The suit/appearance anxiety feeds into the celebrity insecurity theme of the scene.

jokes.text: It's just too damn easy. He looks like a before from Hair Club.
jokes.setup: Williams is discussing why he finds Hank too easy to tease
jokes.punchline: 'A before from Hair Club' is a very specific and devastating visual — Hank as a Hair Club for Men before-photo is both an image and an implication about his hair piece/weave
jokes.explanation: 'A before from Hair Club' is economical and precise. The joke works because Hair Club for Men was a ubiquitous late-night advertiser in this era, making it industry-insider meta while also being a clean visual insult at Hank's expense.

jokes.text: It's just too damn easy. He looks like a before from Hair Club. / I can't go with you on that. I cannot.
jokes.setup: Robin makes the Hair Club joke
jokes.punchline: Larry's ostentatious refusal to pile on — 'I cannot' — while visibly finding it funny, reveals his hypocrisy (he mocks Hank privately all the time)
jokes.explanation: Larry's refusal to join in is its own joke — he's protecting Hank from Robin while having said worse things about Hank privately. 'I cannot' is said with enough strain to make clear how much he wants to agree.

jokes.text: Can I ask you a question? Can you autograph this for my niece, Jennifer. She's six years old. Peter Pan? What? Peter Pan, Mork, whatever.
jokes.setup: Larry has been praising Williams as a legend and great collaborator
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately follows with an autograph request 'for my niece' — the classic talk-show host self-interested move — and then Williams himself can't settle on which character to sign as
jokes.explanation: The autograph-for-my-niece bit exposes Larry's self-interest while Williams' confusion about which character to sign as (Peter Pan vs. Mork) is a nice beat about the complexity of celebrity identity. Both characters are humanized and punctured simultaneously.

jokes.text: My head reminded you of your penis after a cold swim... I was honored.
jokes.setup: Williams apologizes for a crude joke he made at Larry's expense on-air
jokes.punchline: Larry says he was 'honored' by the comparison of his head to a cold-swim penis — a joke that reveals Larry's pathetic desperation to not antagonize his bigger guest
jokes.explanation: Larry calling the penis comparison 'an honor' is a precise skewering of the host-guest power dynamic. The specific image ('after a cold swim' — i.e., shrunken) combined with Larry's eager appeasement is excellent character writing. The joke is simultaneously about Larry's physical insecurity and his professional cowardice. High craft for character integration.

jokes.text: What are you talking about? If I said that, you'd have been pissed off.
jokes.setup: Larry says he was honored by Robin's head-penis comparison; Hank is listening
jokes.punchline: Hank correctly identifies the double standard — if Hank said the same thing, Larry would be furious — revealing Larry's celebrity sycophancy through Hank's jealous lens
jokes.explanation: Hank's observation is completely correct, which makes it both funny and a genuine insight about Larry. The joke operates as character comedy (Hank's jealousy), irony (the truth of his observation), and showbiz satire (stars get away with what staff cannot). Strong character integration.

jokes.text: You're not gonna do Arsenio or Leno, are you? / I've got to. / Fucker. / Hey, it's a business. Get used to it. Blow me.
jokes.setup: Larry confronts Robin about doing other talk shows
jokes.punchline: The exchange escalates from Larry's wounded complaint ('Fucker') to Robin's perfectly calibrated showbiz pragmatism ('Blow me') — both knowing it's business, both performing outrage and resignation
jokes.explanation: A perfect compression of showbiz cynicism. 'Fucker' is Larry at his most unguarded, 'Hey, it's a business. Get used to it. Blow me' is three sentences that contain an entire philosophy. The escalation from complaint to resignation to dismissal in four beats is excellent structure. 'Blow me' as a closing argument in a business conversation is exactly the right tone for this show. Justifies 8+ through economy and character — only these two people, in this relationship, could have this exact exchange.

jokes.text: He's hung like a field mouse. I mean, you pop the diaper and ping! It's like a little sundial. Honey, what time is it? Get the baby. Look, it's 3:00. Oh, 2:30 now. It's real cold.
jokes.setup: Williams is discussing his eight-month-old baby on the talk show
jokes.punchline: Williams riffs on his infant son's anatomy in increasing graphic detail, culminating in using it as a sundial joke — then noting it shrinks in the cold
jokes.explanation: Williams' baby penis riff is characteristically him — it escalates through a dark taboo (infant anatomy) and gets away with it through absurdist specificity ('field mouse,' 'sundial'). The sundial bit is genuinely inventive. The cold-shrinkage callback is a clean button. High impact for a talk show riff.

jokes.text: The trend in talk shows today is not to have a sidekick. Yeah, it is a dying art... but I've been having talks with Dick Cavett about co-hosting.
jokes.setup: Artie is trying to explain the market reality to Hank about sidekick roles
jokes.punchline: Hank counters the dying-art observation with the Cavett co-hosting deal — which we will soon learn is a complete bluff
jokes.explanation: The Cavett bluff plant — which pays off magnificently at episode's end — is effectively seeded here. The joke in the moment is Hank's hopeful namedrop; on rewatch it's tragic. Good structure for the episode's central irony.

jokes.text: What's he doing? He has his own talk show on CNBC. CNBC? What the hell is that? What's that mean? No, my TV stops at channel 13, the way it's supposed to.
jokes.setup: Hank claims Dick Cavett has his own show on CNBC; Artie doesn't know what that is
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'my TV stops at channel 13, the way it's supposed to' is a perfect period-specific character joke about cable TV being an affront to proper television
jokes.explanation: 'My TV stops at channel 13, the way it's supposed to' is an exceptional Artie line — it captures his generational relationship with television as a sacred institution that cable has corrupted. 'The way it's supposed to' is the key phrase: it's not ignorance, it's principled refusal. Perfect economy, strong character integration, and period-specific in a way that is funny even now. One of Artie's best lines in the episode.

jokes.text: Arty, I'm not going anywhere. I got the network by the balls on this one.
jokes.setup: Artie has explained that sidekicks are in a weak market position
jokes.punchline: Hank's blustering confidence — 'I got the network by the balls on this one' — immediately before we cut to him being crushed by the network negotiation is pure dramatic irony
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony of Hank's confidence before the network defeat gives this line rewatch value. The joke is not just in the bluster but in the structure of the scene. Standard blustering character work elevated by what follows.

jokes.text: You sure do keep it dark in here, don't you?
jokes.setup: Larry finds Hank sitting in a darkened office, clearly devastated after the failed negotiation
jokes.punchline: Larry's first observation upon entering is about the lighting — he deflects from the emotional reality with a banal domestic observation, which is both an avoidance tactic and unintentionally poetic
jokes.explanation: A beautiful Larry Sanders beat — faced with genuine emotional vulnerability, Larry's instinct is to comment on the interior design. 'You sure do keep it dark in here, don't you?' is the perfect deflection: banal, slightly paternal, utterly avoidant. It's Larry at his most revealing while seeming most evasive. The economy is excellent.

jokes.text: You sure do keep it dark in here, don't you?
jokes.setup: Hank enters what appears to be a dark office to apologize
jokes.punchline: The observation of the darkness is both literal (he's apparently looking at something — the lawn furniture spots) and metaphorical (the dark mood in the office)
jokes.explanation: A mild observational comment that works as a beat but isn't particularly strong on its own. Texture rather than a punchline.

jokes.text: 'Hey, you untalented, overpriced sidekick, you're just another piece of meat to us, so why don't you take what we gave you last year and be happy with that, you worthless piece of shit?'
jokes.setup: Larry asks what the network said to Hank
jokes.punchline: Hank's paraphrase of the network's position — delivered in escalating corporate cruelty with a perfectly rhythmic close — is obviously an exaggeration but emotionally accurate
jokes.explanation: Hank's paraphrase of the network is both funny and piercing — the escalating insults hit real industry truths about how talent is treated. The rhythm builds well and 'you worthless piece of shit' lands as a genuine gut punch. The joke works because it's half absurdist exaggeration and half documentary truth. Strong character work — only Hank would render his humiliation in such theatrical terms.

jokes.text: Well, I can't do that, can I? ... I've just been on national TV and I've just said, 'Hank Kingsley will not cave in.' So, I am fucked.
jokes.setup: Larry suggests Hank just accept last year's salary since the network won't budge
jokes.punchline: Hank's reason for not being able to accept the deal is that he publicly announced he wouldn't cave — his PR strategy has backed him into an inescapable corner
jokes.explanation: 'So, I am fucked.' — delivered with Hank's specific mixture of clarity and pathos — is one of the episode's great punchlines. The logic is perfect: Hank has publicly committed himself into an impossible position, and his recognition of this is genuinely funny and genuinely tragic. The 'So, I am fucked' is economical and perfectly timed. High character integration: only someone as simultaneously pompous and pathetic as Hank would have engineered this particular trap.

jokes.text: It's gonna be bad enough when this thing hits the front page of Variety. The second page, at least.
jokes.setup: Hank says he can't go to Artie because it would be too embarrassing when this hits Variety
jokes.punchline: Larry corrects him from 'front page' to 'second page, at least' — a gentle but devastating demotion of Hank's self-importance
jokes.explanation: 'The second page, at least' is beautifully constructed. Larry's correction is both an insult and almost consoling — at least Variety will cover it. The economy is near-perfect: three words do the work of a full scene of character dynamics. Hank's expectation of front-page coverage and Larry's matter-of-fact demotion captures their entire relationship. Strong economy and structure scores are justified.

jokes.text: Zip on Cavett. I'm bluffing.
jokes.setup: Larry tries to use the Cavett thing as leverage in Hank's favor
jokes.punchline: Hank admits there is no Cavett deal — he's been bluffing — which mirrors Larry's identical bluff about Nightline that neither of them knew about the other
jokes.explanation: 'Zip on Cavett. I'm bluffing.' is maximally economical — four words to detonate the entire negotiating position. The structure of the episode has been building to this parallel bluff reveal: Hank was doing exactly what Larry was doing, they're mirrors of each other, and neither knew the other's secret. 'Zip' as a word is perfect Hank vocabulary. This is the hinge of the episode's comic structure.

jokes.text: I thought you were bluffing. [long beat] Oh, my God.
jokes.setup: Hank confesses there's no Cavett deal; Larry explains his Nightline offer was real
jokes.punchline: Hank realizes the Nightline offer was genuine — that Larry actually had real leverage all along — and the entire episode's negotiation dynamic collapses into silence
jokes.explanation: This reaction beat is the episode's structural and comedic pinnacle. The entire episode has been building to this mirror: both Hank and Larry have been bluffing about alternative offers, but Larry's was real. The 'Oh, my God' from Hank is the moment of comic recognition — he's been outmaneuvered by the truth. The pause before 'Oh, my God' is where the comedy and the pathos live simultaneously. Exceptional structure across the whole episode — this is the kind of payoff that retroactively improves everything before it.

jokes.text: Jesus, Larry, I could have gotten us a nice table at Musso's. I didn't want anybody to see us, that's all.
jokes.setup: Artie and Larry are meeting covertly on some dark stairs to discuss the Hank situation
jokes.punchline: Artie's complaint about the meeting location — Musso & Frank's (the industry power restaurant) vs. dark stairs — reveals that his primary objection is about the quality of the dinner table, not the secrecy
jokes.explanation: Artie invoking Musso & Frank's as the standard for any meeting is perfect industry-insider character comedy. His complaint about the stairs is less about inconvenience than about the loss of atmosphere and status. Larry's explanation ('I didn't want anybody to see us') and Artie's complete indifference to the discretion rationale is classic.

jokes.text: I have breakfast with Fred Dryer early in the morning. Oh, boy, you must be excited. I bet you won't sleep all night.
jokes.setup: Artie asks Larry to be quick because he has an early breakfast
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'Oh, boy, you must be excited' about breakfast with Fred Dryer (the then-mildly famous actor/TV star) is exaggerated mock-excitement — sarcastically treating Dryer like a major event
jokes.explanation: Fred Dryer is a perfectly chosen name for this joke — minor enough to be mocked but real enough to be specific. 'I bet you won't sleep all night' in flat deadpan is excellent Artie sarcasm. The joke is about the industry habit of treating minor celebrity meetings as major events.

jokes.text: He wants a five percent raise, he wants gross percentage points, he wants three weeks additional paid vacation, and he wants a Hankmobile. What's a Hankmobile? It's that golf cart I told you about last week. I smell urine here.
jokes.setup: Shel is listing Hank's demands; 'Hankmobile' needs explanation
jokes.punchline: After cataloguing significant contract demands, Artie immediately drops 'I smell urine here' — either about the stairs location or a genuine smell — with total incongruity
jokes.explanation: Artie's 'I smell urine here' as a punctuation mark on the contract demands list is a perfect Artie moment — the crass physical reality cutting through the entertainment industry high-mindedness. The juxtaposition of 'Hankmobile' and 'I smell urine' is comic gold. The earlier meeting-on-stairs setup pays this off physically.

jokes.text: He wants a five percent raise, he wants gross percentage points, he wants three weeks additional paid vacation, and he wants a Hankmobile. / What's a Hankmobile? / It's that golf cart I told you about last week. I smell urine here.
jokes.setup: Shel runs through Hank's demands
jokes.punchline: The reveal that 'Hankmobile' is Hank's name for the golf cart — and Artie's non-sequitur 'I smell urine here' immediately after
jokes.explanation: Two jokes in one: (1) The golf cart has graduated to being named — 'Hankmobile' is a perfect distillation of Hank's megalomania applied to a tiny vehicle. (2) Artie's immediate environmental observation ('I smell urine here') as a response to Hank's entire demand list is either literal or deeply metaphorical, and both readings are funny. The 'Hankmobile' naming will pay off even more when Hank actually gets the cart.

jokes.text: Give him everything he wants, or you know what's gonna happen? I'm off the show. I mean it. If he goes, I go, Shel.
jokes.setup: Shel is being pragmatic about Hank's demands; Larry claims to care
jokes.punchline: Larry's threat to leave if Hank leaves is played for comedy because the audience knows Larry cares about the show more than anyone and would never actually leave — it's empty bravado from a man who claims not to care about Hank but clearly does
jokes.explanation: Larry's empty ultimatum is funny because it's so obviously false and yet clearly comes from a real place of caring. The show's central emotional tension — Larry's love for his show and people vs. his inability to express it — is here as comedy.

jokes.text: I can go on after Nightline anytime I want. Call Bob Iger at ABC. He'll tell you.
jokes.setup: Larry is threatening Shel with the Nightline offer as leverage
jokes.punchline: Larry name-drops Bob Iger to add specific credibility to his bluff — which at this point in the episode, neither we nor Shel know is real
jokes.explanation: The Bob Iger namedrop is funny as industry-insider texture and gains huge rewatch value because this turns out to be real — Larry is the only one actually telling the truth. The joke is richer on second viewing.

jokes.text: I don't mean on these stairs. I mean, you know, the network.
jokes.setup: Larry has just said 'I love being here' to Shel during their staircase meeting
jokes.punchline: He immediately clarifies he doesn't mean the stairs — 'I mean, you know, the network' — a tiny self-correction that undercuts his big emotional declaration
jokes.explanation: A subtle but perfectly calibrated Larry Sanders beat. The big emotional statement ('I love being here') is immediately qualified and deflated by the mundane clarification about the stairs. Pure Larry: incapable of letting a sincere moment stand. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: 'Didn't know it was a mannequin.' Look at that. They must love you.
jokes.setup: Hank has apparently received the golf cart (Hankmobile) and there are photos of him with it
jokes.punchline: A caption reading 'Didn't know it was a mannequin' on a photo of Hank with the golf cart — implying something deeply embarrassing about the photo
jokes.explanation: Mysterious and funny — the implication that Hank has been photographed attempting intimacy with a mannequin is left entirely to imagination. Good use of visual gag (the photo) even in transcript form.

jokes.text: Did you get the salary bump? [long pause] Yes.
jokes.setup: Larry inspects the Hankmobile and asks Hank about the negotiation results
jokes.punchline: Hank's long pause before confirming the salary bump — while Larry and the audience wait — signals that everything else did not go as planned; the pause is the joke
jokes.explanation: The pause before 'Yes' tells the entire story. Hank's delay signals relief on only one item, which prepares the audience for the cascade of losses that follows. In a show without a laugh track, this beat of silence is the comedy. The structure is excellent — maximum information with minimum words.

jokes.text: The salary bump was so great that I felt I should give them something. So, you know... I don't need syndication points.
jokes.setup: Larry asks about the syndication points — the big financial item
jokes.punchline: Hank's explanation for giving up syndication points — he got the salary bump and 'felt he should give them something' — is a spectacular self-delusion about how negotiations work
jokes.explanation: 'I felt I should give them something' is one of the episode's best character lines. Hank has entirely internalized the network's negotiating frame — he thinks voluntarily surrendering syndication points is an act of generosity rather than capitulation. The pathos and comedy are perfectly fused. 'I don't need syndication points' delivered with that specific Tambor dignity is the punchline.

jokes.text: What about the vacation? Three weeks? Week and a half.
jokes.setup: Larry is cataloguing what Hank didn't get in the negotiation
jokes.punchline: Three weeks of vacation reduced to 'week and a half' — not even rounding to two — is the escalation of defeats, delivered as matter-of-fact by Hank
jokes.explanation: 'Week and a half' is funnier than 'two weeks' because of its specific, odd non-roundness — it suggests a particularly precise defeat. The escalating revelation of Hank's losses is well-paced.

jokes.text: I had to pay for it myself, so don't tell anybody, okay?
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie admire the Hankmobile golf cart, assuming the network gave it to Hank
jokes.punchline: Hank reveals he bought his own Hankmobile — the one demand he could win was one he had to fund himself
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's most devastating joke and one of its very best. Hank spent the entire episode threatening to walk unless he got his demands, and the one demand he 'won' was the golf cart — which he purchased himself. The gap between his declared triumph and the reality is total. 'Don't tell anybody, okay?' is the perfect button — he's still trying to maintain the illusion of victory. This rivals the best anchor examples in craft: character-specific, earned, structured across the whole episode, and delivered with perfect economy. Tambor's performance makes it land as both comedy and genuine pathos.

jokes.text: You know how I feel about this. You're gonna kiss me this time. No, come on, come on.
jokes.setup: Hank tries to thank Larry physically for going to bat for him; Larry deflects
jokes.punchline: Hank insisting on physical affection (a kiss) from a squirming, avoidant Larry is a brief cringe moment that captures their entire relationship dynamic
jokes.explanation: A brief but characteristic moment — Hank's neediness and Larry's emotional avoidance in physical form. Functional character comedy that serves the relationship dynamic.

jokes.text: The network is fucked, you know that? I lay myself out on the line, and they still don't give Hank everything. What the fuck is that?
jokes.setup: Hank has ridden off happily on his Hankmobile; Larry immediately drops the supportive act
jokes.punchline: Larry's instant pivot from Hank's loyal champion to outraged grievant — the 'network is fucked' declaration — reveals that his loyalty was about his own authority, not Hank
jokes.explanation: Larry's instant mask-drop is a classic Larry Sanders moment. He fought for Hank because the network not following his wishes is the real insult. 'I lay myself out on the line' when he just minutes ago denied doing anything special is perfectly hypocritical. Character integration is excellent.

jokes.text: The poor baby. He seems happy.
jokes.setup: Larry is ranting about the network's failure; Artie observes Hank riding off on his golf cart
jokes.punchline: Artie's dry 'The poor baby. He seems happy.' — offering a contrasting perspective that Hank, despite everything, has achieved a kind of peace — is both cruel and sympathetic
jokes.explanation: 'The poor baby. He seems happy.' is exceptional Artie economy. Five words contain the entire episode's emotional arc: pity for Hank, recognition of his limited victory, and a gentle rebuke to Larry's grievance. The contrast between 'poor baby' (condescending) and 'he seems happy' (almost envious) is the comedy. Only Artie can deliver this as the final word on the situation.

jokes.text: That is not the issue. You'd think the network would care enough about me to do what I tell them. It's an insult. This is an insult.
jokes.setup: Artie points out that Hank seems happy anyway
jokes.punchline: Larry explicitly frames Hank's unsatisfactory deal as a personal insult to LARRY — the complete narcissistic inversion is the punchline
jokes.explanation: Larry has pivoted from 'I care about Hank' to 'the network disrespected ME by not doing what I said' in about 30 seconds. The speed and clarity of this narcissistic pivot is excellent. 'The network would care enough about ME' is the tell.

jokes.text: You did have that offer to go on after Nightline, didn't you? [pause] Fuck no.
jokes.setup: Artie mentions the network should be nervous about Larry's Nightline offer
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'Fuck no' — admitting the Nightline offer was also a bluff — is the episode's final and perfectly placed revelation, collapsing the entire negotiating premise
jokes.explanation: The episode's final joke is its best-constructed moment and earns the highest scores. The entire episode has been building to this: Larry insisted on the Nightline offer as his trump card (02:41, 24:33), confronted Hank's Cavett bluff (23:04), only to reveal his own offer was equally fictional. 'Fuck no' is two words that retroactively reframe everything — both men were bluffing, neither had leverage, and the show goes on anyway. The structural payoff is extraordinary: the episode's thesis about show-business performance and self-delusion is stated and then detonated in a single breath. 'Fuck no' is perfectly Shandling's Larry — the one moment of total honesty, delivered with exhausted matter-of-factness to Artie, the only person he'd be honest with. The pause before it is the comedy. This is the episode's 9.5+ anchor moment.

tmdb_overview: It's contract negotiation time for Hank and he's going for a raise ... and a golf cart.
